items.title: Last Night in Surulere
native: Did you catch the match at Femi Adebayo's place in Surulere last night?
I thought we'd watch quietly, but half the building ended up joining us.
His sister Bisi brought jollof rice, and I took some fried plantain.
Everyone was still finding a seat when Arsenal scored their first goal.
Femi jumped up so quickly that his cushion landed in my dinner.
We spent most of the second half arguing about that missed penalty.
Even my aunt put her phone away for the last few minutes.
When Arsenal finally won, you could hear cheering all along our street.
Next time, come over early so we can save you a decent seat.

items.title: A Rainy First Day
native: My first morning at a new school in Dublin began with a soaking.
I'd missed the bus in Rathmines and walked through the rain without a coat.
My timetable was so wet that the ink had started to run.
A girl called Aoife Byrne found me studying a map beside the lockers.
She lent me a dry sweater and walked me to our classroom.
Our teacher asked about my old school, but I was so nervous I could barely answer.
Aoife moved her bag off the next chair and waved me over.
At lunchtime, we shared her cheese sandwiches and laughed about my squeaky shoes.
By the final bell, I knew the route home and had a friend.

items.title: Dad's New Phone
native: Dad, let's set up your new phone here at the kitchen table.
Plug the charger into the wall, then connect the cable to your phone.
Press the power button and choose English when the language list appears.
Select our home Wi-Fi network and enter the password from the router sticker.
When the phone asks, follow the prompts to copy everything from your old phone.
Keep both phones nearby until the transfer finishes, even if it takes a while.
Once that's done, I'll move your SIM card across and check your mobile connection.
Open WhatsApp and send Auntie Mei a message to check it's working.
Finally, let's make the text larger so your shopping list is easier to read.

items.title: Dinner Delivered in Tiong Bahru
native: I tried GrabFood from my flat in Tiong Bahru on Tuesday.
The chicken rice arrived warm, and the soup hadn't leaked into the bag.
I liked seeing the rider's location without having to send extra messages.
The delivery fee was S$4, which felt steep for such a short trip.
Still, the app showed that charge before I confirmed my order.
One photo made the portion look bigger than it actually was.
I'd rather see a plain picture that matches what turns up.
For rainy evenings, the convenience probably makes the extra cost worth it.
I'll use it again, but I'll compare the final totals more carefully.

items.title: Checking a School Fee Receipt
native: Hello, I'm calling about my daughter Zoya Naidoo's school fee receipt.
She's in grade 3, and her teacher is Nomsa Khumalo.

items.title: Melbourne's Football Weekends
native: In Melbourne, plenty of people plan their weekends around Australian rules football.
At the Melbourne Cricket Ground, fans often arrive well before the opening bounce.
Fans wear their club scarves on trains and trams on the way to the match.
The game uses an oval ball, and players can kick or handball it.
An untouched kick through the tall central posts scores 6 points.
The crowd gets louder when the scores are close in the last few minutes.
Support for clubs like Collingwood and Carlton often runs in the family.
Many fans also follow local teams, and volunteers run the canteens at their grounds.
At local matches, catching up with friends is often as important as the game itself.
